t.16.1: Aṣṭāvakra said: My dear son, you may expound or listen to various scriptures again and again, yet you will not find abiding in the Self except through forgetting everything.
t.16.3: Everyone is miserable because of exertion, yet no one understands this. By this very teaching alone, the fortunate one attains final bliss.
t.16.2: Whether you enjoy pleasures, perform actions, or practice samādhi, O wise one, still only a mind from which all desires have been cast out will delight you beyond measure.
t.16.4: Happiness belongs to that master of idleness who is wearied even by the activity of closing and opening his eyes, and to no one else.
t.16.5: When the mind is freed from such pairs of opposites as "this is done" and "this is not done," then it becomes indifferent to dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
t.16.6: The dispassionate man hates the objects of sense, while the passionate man craves them; but one who is free from both grasping and letting go is neither dispassionate nor passionate.
t.16.8: In engagement attachment arises, and in withdrawal aversion indeed arises. The wise one, free from the pairs of opposites like a child, remains established just as he is.
t.16.7: As long as desire lives, desire that is the abode of the state without discrimination, so long does the sense of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted remain, the sprout of the spreading tree of saṃsāra.
t.16.9: The one full of attachment wishes to abandon saṃsāra out of a desire to be rid of suffering. But one free from attachment is without suffering and is not distressed even in the midst of it.
t.16.10: He who has pride even in liberation, and likewise a sense of 'mine' even toward the body, is neither a man of knowledge nor a yogī; he is merely a partaker of suffering.
t.16.11: Even if Hara, Hari, or the lotus-born one were your teacher, still you would find no abiding in your true self except through forgetting everything.
